sentences.t: The data center proposed at 1500 Woodlawn Drive in Baltimore County, Maryland, would go on the site that was the Social Security Administration's home until 2023, and for thirty years before that was where a large part of Woodlawn worked.
The complex once employed about 10,000 people, and it also housed the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
A dedicated Social Security data center ran on the site from 1980 to 2010, drawing five megawatts, 1.2 of them from solar, before it was turned into office space.
The proposal now is a 42 acre, 150 megawatt data center, thirty times the power the old government data center used.
The owner is Security Land and Development Co, which has held the property for decades.
Deed records from 2003 name the 1500 Woodlawn Limited Partnership, Harry W Rogers III, William A Rodgers, W Dale Hess and Regency Affiliates Inc, and the partnership's registration lapsed in 2023.
The company has no data center experience, and Nature Forward suggests it may be seeking permits to sell the entitled land on rather than build.
The plan includes giving five acres to BGE for an electrical substation.
Construction is estimated at about 1,000 temporary jobs, and the finished data center would need fewer than 100 permanent staff.
Woodlawn is between 77 and 79 percent non-white, with a median household income of $82,466 against $91,768 for the county, and roughly a fifth of residents have limited English.
It already carries higher than average exposure to fine particulate matter, ozone and road traffic.
At a neighbourhood meeting on December 2, 2025, hosted by state senator Charles Sydnor III, residents asked about water use, house prices and utility bills, and got no clear answers.
On February 3, 2026 the Baltimore County Council voted unanimously for Bill 3-26, a freeze on data center permits introduced by councilman Pat Young and co-sponsored by six colleagues.
It holds permits for 90 days after the Planning Board delivers its study and cannot run past January 1, 2027.

Young told the council: "A year and a half ago, when someone said data center, what we thought in our minds did not include what we found out now: the impact on infrastructure, the impact on water, the impact on power. It makes sense for a moratorium, in my opinion."
No permit had been filed for the Woodlawn site before the vote.

The developer's lawyer, Christopher Mudd, had told the council the week before that his client was "nearing an agreement with a data center operator to back the project", and joined others in asking for a shorter moratorium.
The project is put at 150 megawatts on 42 acres, proposed, with no year and no named developer.
The nearest large power stations are Brandon Shores, a 1,273 megawatt coal plant 24 kilometres away, and the 841 megawatt Herbert A Wagner station 25 kilometres off.

unconfirmed: No operator has been named, and whether the agreement Mudd referred to was signed is unknown. Water use has not been disclosed, nor the type of generation the 150 megawatts would draw on. The current legal owner of the site is unclear given the lapsed partnership registration. Nothing in the Banner report says the Woodlawn site was exempted from Bill 3-26, but neither does it say it was named, so the earlier flat statement that it was not exempted has come out. Our record does not carry the Baltimore County moratorium among nearby measures, which is an omission: Bill 3-26 applies to permits across the county.

sentences.t: This data center would sit on the sea floor, in the Western Passage off Eastport, in Washington County, Maine.

DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC wants to put server pods underwater there, powered by tidal turbines, and filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on February 11, 2026 for a 48 month preliminary permit to study the site.
The first deployment as filed would have held 170 turbines and 34 data center pods at 51 megawatts.
After the commission found the filing deficient, the company cut the operational envelope from 400 acres to 27.1 acres and the power from 51 megawatts to 15.
The man behind it is Louis Wolfson, a luxury real estate developer from Massachusetts and the managing member of DeepGreen Holdings LLC.
Wolfson has written that he hopes to build the project with local cooperation and an emphasis on trust and environmental stewardship.
The company is pursuing a second underwater project in Alaska's Upper Cook Inlet.
Eastport did not take to it.

At the city council on May 13, 2026, Suellen Hendrix said of Wolfson, "This man is a one-percenter", and "He doesn't care about us", and asked why he was not building it near his own home in Massachusetts.

Birdy Velveteen raised protected wetlands affected by the onshore cables and possible breaches of Maine's Mandatory Shoreland Zoning Act, and Laurie Stone questioned a community benefits agreement the city said it knew nothing about.
Deborah Gillespie drafted a sample moratorium ordinance from state templates.

That night the council voted to send a letter of objection rather than impose a moratorium; the Washington County Commission had already written on April 9 that this type of project "would be too risky for this region and its waters and the people of Washington County who live and work here".
Three months later the council went further.

On August 13, 2026 it voted unanimously for a 180 day moratorium on any application, permit, licence or approval for a commercial or industrial data center or AI computing facility, covering land-based, underwater, partly or fully submerged installations and their supporting infrastructure.
Councillor Karen Raye made the motion.

Birdy Velveteen, speaking for the Eastport Coalition for Healthy Oceans, said the group had watched data center trends and seen that many "try to circumvent local bans by calling themselves things like 'co-location storage facilities'", and that its updated petitions were meant to keep matters in residents' hands, so that "We the People keep approval power over future large-scale development."
Chris Gardner, executive director of the Eastport Port Authority, was more open to it: "If the Port Authority is so inclined to say we want to partner with an AI company, our charter allows it."
The moratorium did not stop the federal process.

On August 21, 2026, eight days after the vote, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission accepted DeepGreen's filing as complete, which is a procedural step rather than a grant of the permit, and set October 19 as the deadline for public comments and motions to intervene.
The downsized project is put at $100 million, 15 megawatts and about 27 acres of the bay.
The entry now carries 15 megawatts, down from the 51 first filed.
The Eastport moratorium runs from August 14, 2026 to February 14, 2027.
No other data center site is recorded anywhere in Washington County, and no grid control area is recorded for this location.
The nearest power station of any size is the 64 megawatt Woodland Pulp biomass plant, 38 kilometres away.

unconfirmed: The cost figure differs between accounts: our record carries $415 million, which belongs to the original 51 megawatt, 400 acre proposal, while the Bangor Daily News gives $100 million for the downsized project, and that is the figure used above. Whether a city moratorium reaches a project in federal and state waters at all is unresolved, and the preliminary permit itself has not been granted, only the application accepted as complete. The Passamaquoddy Tribe's position and the effect on the weir and fishing grounds of the Western Passage were not established from the sources we read. The Maine Monitor account of the August council meeting would not load on this pass, so the vote and the quotations from it are taken from WABI, which dates the adoption to August 14 while the council met the evening before. We could not reach DeepGreen for comment and the company had not publicly responded to the moratorium.

sentences.t: Lewiston said no.

On December 16, 2025 the city council in Lewiston, in Androscoggin County, Maine, voted unanimously against a proposal by MillCompute LLC to put an AI data center into Bates Mill No 3, the historic mill building in the middle of town.
The plan was for 85,000 square feet of servers alongside office and innovation space for technology companies.
What sank it was the money.
The deal included a 20 year tax increment financing agreement that would have returned 90 percent of the project's taxes to the developer for ten years, then 85 percent for the following decade.
More than 100 emails of public comment were filed against it.
Ward 6 councillor David Chittim said: "This had the potential for being a great project. It may still have, but not within the time frames and the constraints that have been imposed on it."

Hunter Bouchard, the sophomore class president at Lewiston High School, told the council he had talked to as many classmates as he could and all of them were against it: "I want to remind you who they are. These are not just high school students; this is the next generation. They are going to be affected by this change 10 and 20 years down the line."

City administrator Bryan Kaenrath, who had supported the project for the tax revenue, said afterwards that future proposals would have to be looked at "very carefully": "There are many other options for development in these buildings. Making them financially feasible is the biggest challenge."
The project is recorded as cancelled, at a cost of $300 million, with no capacity figure.
Nothing is recorded about who owns MillCompute LLC, and the council was not told.
Lewiston's vote came before the wave of Maine moratoriums it now sits among: Wiscasset from November 2025, then Westbrook, Scarborough and Brunswick in the first week of June 2026.
No other data center site is recorded anywhere in Androscoggin County.
The nearest large generator is the 827 megawatt William F Wyman oil-fired plant, 39 kilometres south.

unconfirmed: The power demand of the proposal was never published and the Maine Public report does not give one. Who is behind MillCompute LLC, and whether the company has gone anywhere else in Maine since, we could not establish. The $300 million cost in our record is not confirmed by the source we read. The News Center Maine report of the same vote, also in our record, would give the exact vote count and more councillor names; we did not fetch it and the count is left as unanimous, which is what Maine Public reports.

sentences.t: The data center at Old Ferry Road never got as far as a planning application, and it still cost Wiscasset $240,000 meant for housing.
The 300 acres opposite the remains of Maine Yankee, in Lincoln County, Maine, once belonged to the atomic power company, and the town bought them in 2013.
Wiscasset has about 4,000 residents.
On November 5, 2024 Lincoln County awarded the town $240,000 of American Rescue Plan money for a feasibility study on affordable housing, against a proposal for 110 units.
Two days later the town's economic development director, Aaron Chrostowsky, began discussing a data center for the same land.

On February 4, 2025 he told a regional planning staffer he intended to use the federal housing money to study a data center instead; the staffer warned him against misappropriating government funding, and he asked for secrecy.
By March 3, 2025 the county had noticed the plans had significantly changed, and town manager Dennis Simmons defended the pivot on March 24.
The county withheld the money on March 27 and formally rescinded it on May 29, 2025, saying it no longer had confidence in the town's housing commitment.
On August 19, 2025 the town signed a nondisclosure agreement with an unnamed California site evaluator, and the plans became public the following month.
Protect Wiscasset formed to oppose the project, co-founded by Richard Davis, alongside RePower Wiscasset, started by Peter Arnold to push renewable energy on the Maine Yankee land.
A public survey run for a state economic recovery programme in January 2025 had found residents wanted parks, shops and culture on the land, not technology.
As of May 2026 nothing had been built.
Chrostowsky said he had not heard from the site evaluator since talks paused in November 2025.
On March 3, 2026 Lincoln County gave the $240,000 to Waldoboro and Newcastle instead.

Commissioner Evan Goodkowsky said Wiscasset would not be a power player in any new housing project for years; Peter Arnold said the episode still clouds other development and has eroded trust in the town's governance.
Wiscasset adopted a pause on data center proposals on November 4, 2025, one of the earliest in Maine.
The entry stands as a proposal, with no developer, no capacity and no year.

unconfirmed: No company has ever been named. The $5 billion figure attached to the development in the reporting is the town's characterisation of what was discussed, not a filed or verified number, and no power or water demand was ever published. Whether the California site evaluator is still interested is unknown; the last contact reported is November 2025. The News Center Maine report on resident concerns, which would add named residents from the town meetings, returned HTTP 403 and could not be read.

sentences.t: More than 125 people came to the Allen Park planning commission in Wayne County, Michigan, on January 8, 2026, and about 40 of them spoke.
Almost all opposed the data center.
The meeting ran four hours and ended with the commission voting to postpone its decision, with commissioner Fred Frank the only vote against the delay.
Solstice Data wants to build a 26 megawatt data center of about 45,000 square feet on Enterprise Drive, south of I-94, opening in the first quarter of 2027 with 30 to 35 staff on site.
Backup power would come from 12 generators with 12 above ground fuel tanks, and the company says cooling would be a closed loop, with municipal water used only for the offices.
The site sits beside the Ecorse River with the Reeck Drain crossing its southern edge, and the developers say regulated wetlands may be present and are running a delineation study.
The questions residents asked were about bills.
Abbas Alawieh, a candidate for the Michigan Senate, put it directly: "There is an elephant in the room: will this raise our rates?"

Joanna Whaley, a candidate for the Michigan House, said: "The corporations are doing really well right now, and all the rest of us are doing worse and having to make decisions about what bill we might pay."
Asked whether the plant would cause air pollution, Solstice Data chief executive Phil Harvey said it would not.
Before the hearing, Indivisible: Downriver United 734 organised a protest outside.

Areje Anderson, the company's chief of people, said: "At this stage, we're focused on ensuring the local community and relevant stakeholders have the opportunity to engage with us directly through the formal planning and zoning process."

The commission asked for more before it would decide: a further sound study, an assessment by the fire department, outreach to neighbouring communities, and more detail on planning and water use, as its consultants at Carlisle Wortman recommended.
By local standards this is a small project.
Its 26 megawatts is about a fiftieth of the 1.4 gigawatt data center proposed in Saline Township.
The entry is recorded as blocked, at 26 megawatts.
Thirteen municipalities in and around Wayne and Washtenaw counties have data center moratoriums or zoning limits, among them Taylor, next door, from January 20, 2026.
The 739 megawatt Dearborn Industrial Generation gas plant is six kilometres away.

unconfirmed: What happened after the postponement is not established: we found no report of the additional sound study, the fire department assessment or a later commission vote, and our record's "blocked" status is not explained by any source we read. The city's own project page and the consultants' report to the planning commission are in our record as sources but were not fetched. Whether the wetland delineation found regulated wetlands is unknown. Solstice Data's backers and its customers are not named anywhere we read. Phil Harvey's answer on air pollution is the reporter's account of what he said rather than a quotation, and is no longer given as one.

sentences.t: On August 4, 2026, Augusta Township, in Washtenaw County, Michigan, voted the data center down, 2,314 to 269.
That is 89.5 percent against.
The vote overturned the rezoning of seven parcels, more than 500 acres of farmland near Milan, from agricultural residential to general industrial, and left the land zoned as it was.

The project was Thor Equities', a New York real estate firm, and it covered 822 acres of farmland and wetland southeast of Ann Arbor, with at least five large buildings for artificial intelligence and computing, potentially for a company such as Google or Microsoft.
It might have used a million gallons of water a day, and would have had large diesel generators.

A second account of the vote, from WEMU, puts it at roughly nine to one and records that the ballot question existed only because residents had gathered the signatures to put it there, after the township board approved the rezoning in July 2025.
The township board had been entirely in favour.
It approved the rezoning unanimously in July 2025, despite the objections already being made.
Township clerk Kim Gonczy said of the project: "It would just be so huge for us."
Officials played down the concerns, saying lighting would be directed at the ground and the noise ordinance would be complied with.
Travis Matts, who learned of the proposal in May 2025, set up Protect Augusta Charter Township and went door to door.
In about two weeks in August 2025 the group collected 957 signatures, well above the 561 needed to force a referendum, from an estimated 1,200 to 1,400 residents contacted.
Matts said: "It's sad that we residents have to fight as hard as we do to keep these facilities out of our backyards, but if we don't then who will?"
Another opponent, Deborah Fuqua-Frey, described the response to the campaign as harassment: "Calling the cops, that's harassment."
The residents were not finished after the vote.
Petitions were submitted to recall all seven township trustees, under review for a possible place on the November ballot.

Wendy Taylor Albers, who organised the petition, said the vote itself had been the point: "But I would have accepted anything that the residents of Augusta Township decided. This was all about giving the people of the township a voice in this rezoning decision. So, I'm ecstatic."
The project is now recorded as blocked, on 822 acres, at a cost of $1 billion, with no capacity figure.

The land sits in the middle of a cluster: the OpenAI Stargate campus at Saline is 17 kilometres away at 1,400 megawatts, a Google project at 2,700 megawatts is 23 kilometres off, and fifteen municipalities nearby carry moratoriums or zoning limits.
The 3,080 megawatt Monroe coal plant is 33 kilometres south.

unconfirmed: The acreage differs between accounts: Bridge Michigan describes an 822 acre development, our record carries the same figure, and the ballot question covered seven parcels of just over 500 acres, so the referendum may not have covered the whole site. The exact date of the board's rezoning vote differs too, given as July 1, 2025 by Bridge Michigan and July 22, 2025 elsewhere; neither could be confirmed against the ordinance, and Bridge Michigan itself gives only the month. Whether Thor Equities has abandoned the project, or intends to seek rezoning again, is unknown, as is the identity of any end user. Neither source names a capacity in megawatts.

sentences.t: Microsoft asked Gaines Township to rezone five parcels, nearly 104 acres along Patterson Avenue SE and 76th Street SE near Caledonia, in Kent County, Michigan, to light industrial for a data center campus south of Grand Rapids.
The company already owns about 320 acres of industrially zoned land nearby.
The planning commission held its public hearing on April 16, 2026 in the auditorium of South Christian High School, because the township hall would not hold the crowd.
Hundreds came, many of them against.
A large group representing a local building trades union spoke in favour, and one resident called the project a generational investment.
Another asked how any condition could be enforced against a company worth trillions of dollars.
After several hours the commission voted to table its decision, with no timetable set.
The township attorney said it was not clear whether another special meeting would be scheduled or the item would return on a regular agenda.
Any recommendation would then go to the township board, which would hold its own hearing before a final vote.
Microsoft said it was proud to be part of the Gaines Township community, and would not confirm whether the buildings would support artificial intelligence.
It promised not to draw on local groundwater and to pay for the water and electrical infrastructure upgrades the campus would need, without giving figures.

This was not the first attempt: on February 4, 2026 Microsoft wrote asking the township to move a public hearing set for February 12 to late March, saying its plans continued to evolve on size, scope and design and that it was organising a community meeting for early March.
The site is recorded at 414 acres with no capacity figure, proposed.
Microsoft has a second proposal 15 kilometres away in Dorr Township, where a twelve month moratorium is in force, and a third at Lowell, listed as suspended at 100 megawatts.
Generation nearby is thin: the 843 megawatt Zeeland gas station lies 36 kilometres off and the 1,331 megawatt J H Campbell coal plant 53 kilometres away.

unconfirmed: No power figure has been made public for the Gaines Township campus, and Microsoft will not say what the buildings are for. The acreage in our record, 414, does not match the 104 acres in the rezoning request, and appears to combine that with the 316 acre former Steelcase site Microsoft bought nearby in 2024; the true campus extent is unclear. A line saying Microsoft had been buying residential properties in the area came out: no source we read says so, and the February 2026 postponement it was tied to was asked for on the ground that the design was still changing. Whether the commission has voted since April 16, 2026 is unknown; the report we read leaves it tabled indefinitely. No named residents or commissioners were quoted in the source.

sentences.t: The people of Solon Township, in Kent County, Michigan, learned about the data center from the news.
A technology company operating through a shell called Venerly LLC has been looking at farmland north of Grand Rapids and just outside Cedar Springs, under the name Project Peninsula.
Fox 17 places the land just west of US-131, between 16 and 17 Mile roads, next to the Cedarfield neighbourhood, most of it zoned agricultural and residential.
The Right Place, the region's economic development agency, says a few leading United States technology companies are looking at the site and are in due diligence and planning, and will not name them.
No formal proposal has been submitted to the township.
The domain projectpeninsula.com was registered and Venerly LLC incorporated in March 2024.

Township supervisor Bob Ellick signed a nondisclosure agreement with Venerly on June 11, 2025 and remained bound by it until December 23, 2025, and what he learned in that period is sealed for five years, until 2030.
The public found out in January 2026, and opposition began then.
By then the groundwork was laid.
The township had amended its master plan in December 2024 and passed zoning amendments for industrial and commercial use in October 2025.
Developers proposed drawing two million gallons a day per region, across three planned regions.
The site is Moore's Farm, spanning Solon and Algoma townships.

In February 2026 the township passed a six month moratorium on data centers, extended in July 2026, when it also banned future officials from signing nondisclosure agreements and hired new legal counsel.

It has refused or tabled public baseline water testing, numerical limits on water withdrawal, disclosure of conflicts of interest, ongoing public emissions reporting, and the rezoning of 17 Mile Road, which waits on a master plan review.
Neighbours are split.
Bruce Jenvey said: "This is a very peaceful country, like a setting to live in, lots of wildlife, very low light pollution."
Don Bowerman said: "I would probably move if they put a data center back there, or even if they put a housing development back there."
Ariadne Winquist takes the other view: "I do see it as progress. And my kids are all in for all the data, the computer stuff."
The entry is recorded at 800 acres and $1 billion, proposed, with the developer given as "Venerly LLC?" and no capacity figure.
The only other data center site within 40 kilometres is the Switch campus at Grand Rapids, 31 kilometres away.

unconfirmed: The end user is unknown and deliberately so; the only thing reported about it is that it is not Microsoft. The power demand has never been stated. The timeline used here is published by Stop Solon Township Data Center, a campaign group opposed to the project, and we have relied on it for dates and township actions that we could not check against township minutes; where it characterises motives rather than records an action, we have not repeated it. The Venerly LLC name, the Project Peninsula name and the 800 acre figure were credited to the Fox 17 report, which carries none of them; they come from the campaign timeline and our own record, and are now sourced there. Fox 17 gives only a location between 16 and 17 Mile roads west of US-131.

sentences.t: Microsoft bought the land for its Dorr Township data center, in Allegan County, Michigan, before anyone locally knew what it was for.
The company bought more than 272 acres of farmland off 144th Avenue near US-131 in late 2024, paying close to $150,000 an acre.
On March 4, 2026 the township board approved a twelve month moratorium on data center development, by four votes to two.
Treasurer Sheila Reitz, clerk Debbie Sewers and trustees Pat Champion and Dan Weber voted for it; supervisor Jeff Miling and trustee John Tuinstra voted against, preferring a shorter pause.
More than 75 residents filled the new township hall auditorium and cheered the vote.
Rhonda Winters told the board: "Until we have proof that it's not a detriment, I would ask that we put a pause on it."
Rachael Halpely said: "We need to make sure we have local control over these data centers. It's not unreasonable."
Nick Barlow wanted more than a pause: "I don't want a moratorium ... I just don't want the damn thing to go in ... period."
The moratorium is meant to give the township time to study the question and write zoning rules, and runs to about March 2027.
Residents had been turning out since the plan became known: more than five dozen filled a township board meeting on December 18, 2025 to ask about traffic, electricity and the water supply.
The Dorr site is recorded at 272 acres, proposed, with no capacity figure.
Microsoft's other West Michigan proposal, at Gaines Township, is 15 kilometres away, and a suspended Microsoft-linked project at Lowell is 30 kilometres off.
Five municipalities within reach of the site carry data center moratoriums, including Dorr itself, Oshtemo, Texas Township, Allendale and Portage.
The 843 megawatt Zeeland gas station is 27 kilometres away and the 1,331 megawatt J H Campbell coal plant 46 kilometres.

unconfirmed: Microsoft has published no capacity, building count or timetable for Dorr, and it is not clear whether the company has applied for anything. The moratorium date is a discrepancy: our record gives February 26, 2026 while the newspaper it cites reports the board vote on March 4, 2026. The purchase price is another: search results and trade summaries give about $48 million for the 272 acres, but the reports we could read give only the acreage and a rate of close to $150,000 an acre, so the rate is what stands above. The WZZM report on the Dorr protests returned HTTP 403 on this pass, and with it the line about long-time resident Linda Dumond pressing the planning commission, which no source we could read carries; the resident turnout is now taken from the Wilcox account of the December 18, 2025 board meeting. Whether the moratorium has been challenged, and what the township's study has concluded, are unknown.

sentences.t: The complaint about the data center at 415 East Prairie Ronde Street in Dowagiac, in Cass County, Michigan, is a sound.
Mitchell Gourley, who lives near the plant, describes it this way: "It's almost like having a vacuum cleaner running all the time."
Philip Cunningham said he started hearing it randomly, out of nowhere.
Neighbours report 60 to 70 decibels in front of the facility, about the level of an air conditioner or a dishwasher running without stopping.

Residents have brought a class action against Alliance Cloud Services LLC, a subsidiary of Hyperscale Data Inc, alleging the plant has emitted and continues to emit unreasonable and excessive noise from its cooling fans, with insufficient barriers.
Dowagiac revised its noise ordinance in March 2026.
Gourley says what he wants is simple: "I would just like there would be less noise."
On July 13, 2026 Hyperscale's chief executive, Will Horne, came to a public meeting.

He said all cryptocurrency mining at the site would stop within three months and the plant would pivot to artificial intelligence computing and robot training, and that noise should fall considerably as a result.
He told the room: "I want something better for my kids, and I'm sure everyone here wants something better for theirs."
The company offered to buy the homes of residents on nearby Louise Avenue who were unhappy with the plant.
The room was not soothed.
One resident asked: "How is this better for our community?"
A homeowner told Horne: "Your business has been sneaky, uncooperative with local ordinances, and dismissive of Dowagiac's concerns regarding the impact of the noise."
Another asked why, if it was such a good idea for Dowagiac, he had not built it in his own back yard.
Mayor Patrick Bakeman was more willing, saying that if the noise came down and the work came with it, "I think that would be the best scenario for everybody."
The plant is getting bigger while the argument goes on.
Hyperscale has bought more than 48 acres to expand, and says the transition will create about 500 jobs.
The site is recorded as operating at 30 megawatts on 34 acres.
Seven jurisdictions around it carry data center moratoriums or zoning limits, including Penn, Porter and Lincoln townships, all adopted between May and June 2026.
The 2,177 megawatt Donald C Cook nuclear station is 39 kilometres away, and the 1,082 megawatt Indeck Niles gas plant 18 kilometres.

unconfirmed: The court and filing date of the class action were not given in the report we read, and we could not establish how many plaintiffs it covers or its current stage. The decibel limits in the revised Dowagiac ordinance, and the fines said to have been levied against the plant, were reported in summaries we did not read directly, so the numbers are left out. The street address comes from our own record; the WWMT reports do not give it. Whether cryptocurrency mining has in fact stopped since July 2026, and whether the noise has fallen, are unknown. The MLive report on living next to the plant, which is in our record and would carry more resident detail, could not be fetched. Hyperscale's planned expanded capacity is not stated anywhere we read; our record's 30 megawatts is the existing figure.
